beats.narration_text: Hello, I am Muskan Agrawal, and this video is a summary of Week Three of the Humanitarians AI website restructure: a stakeholder insight plan, a full set of discussion questions, and the beginnings of a structural hierarchy strategy for the homepage.

Two weeks of auditing produced a specification: a type scale, a contrast target, a line length. Every one of those is a decision design can make on its own. This week is about the decisions it cannot.
beats.new_visual_element: White card — what the numbers already settled, ticked off

beats.narration_text: A measurement can tell you the hero is media heavy. It cannot tell you who the site is for. That is not a design question. It belongs to the organization.
beats.new_visual_element: Black card — A NUMBER CAN'T CHOOSE AN AUDIENCE

beats.act: SCENE 2 — What only the organization can answer
beats.narration_text: The week started by counting who the homepage is for. It speaks to eight different audiences: fellows and international graduates, donors, mentors, educators, partner organizations, children and families, volunteers, and the general public. Eight audiences, one page, no stated order of priority.
beats.new_visual_element: Eight audience rows with measured mention counts

beats.act: SCENE 2 — What only the organization can answer
beats.narration_text: Then the vocabulary. The homepage runs about twelve hundred words and carries twenty four named concepts a first time reader has to decode. Tier One. Tiers Three to Six. Irreducibly Human. Botspeak. Addams. Roughly one piece of internal shorthand every fifty words.
beats.new_visual_element: Tier framework screenshot, the three tier cards boxed, count chip

shot.hold_reason: card boxes measured from 02_tier_framework.jpg pixels — see SHOTLIST.md

beats.act: SCENE 2 — What only the organization can answer
beats.narration_text: And the exits. Thirteen separate learn more and explore links leave the homepage. Thirteen equally weighted onward paths is thirteen ways to leave and no way to be led.
beats.new_visual_element: Three stat blocks — 13 onward links, 69 clickable labels, 54 distinct

beats.act: SCENE 2 — What only the organization can answer
beats.narration_text: The same page makes three asks at once, side by side and identically weighted: donate now, volunteer, watch on YouTube. Which of those matters most is not a question a designer can answer.
beats.new_visual_element: Mission CTA screenshot, the three-button group boxed

beats.narration_text: For a donor, the trust picture is mixed. The site states its five oh one c three status and its E I N. It does not publish an annual report, a Form nine ninety, a named board, or a third party charity rating.
beats.new_visual_element: Two-column ledger — on the page vs not on the page

beats.narration_text: And one finding needs an answer before any of it gets designed. The homepage says one hundred percent of donations fund the programs, mentorship and project support. The footer of the same page says one hundred percent of all donations support direct operational costs, including legal fees and staff salaries. Both cannot be the promise.
beats.new_visual_element: The two quoted claims, stacked, with the conflict marked

beats.narration_text: Success metrics are the other gap. Every number on the homepage is a tier label, a legal identifier, a chapter count or a copyright year. Not one of them is an outcome. No fellows placed. No tools delivered.
beats.new_visual_element: Inventory of every number on the page, and what each one is

beats.narration_text: None of those are design decisions. Every one of them is an organizational decision that a designer can surface, but should not make alone. So the next step is to ask.

The output of this week is a discussion guide: a structured set of open questions for stakeholders, mentors and donors, across eight themes. Audience priority. First impression. Primary action. Terminology. Navigation. Tone. Trust. And success metrics.
beats.new_visual_element: The eight themes, listed with marks

beats.narration_text: On audience and message: if a first time visitor reads one sentence and leaves, what should that sentence have told them? Which single audience matters most this quarter? And what do people most often misunderstand about what this organization does?

On action and language: if a visitor does exactly one thing, what should it be? Which of these named concepts would you keep if a stranger had to understand the page without help? And which navigation links exist because someone still needs them?

On trust and proof: what would a donor need to see to give with confidence? What is the one number that would show this year was worth funding? And where should the writing sound like a research group, and where like a program a family could join?

Alongside the questions, the structural hierarchy strategy took shape. The principle is the one the audit kept pointing at: lead with what a visitor came looking for, and let what the organization offers follow from that.
beats.new_visual_element: Four-step content order, built step by step

beats.narration_text: That hierarchy work fed one more round of hero refinement. It stays a direction, not a layout, deliberately. The hero should not be redrawn until the people who own the message have said which message leads.
beats.new_visual_element: Statement card — the hero stays a direction

shot.hold_reason: No proposed hero layout is drawn anywhere in this series. Carried forward from the Week 2 correction.

beats.narration_text: Week One was the audit. Week Two was the specification. Week Three is the questions, and the meeting they are for. Week Four moves to navigation cleanup with the developer, and to agreeing how design and development hand work over.
beats.new_visual_element: Title card — the four-week arc, with Week 4 named as nav cleanup and handoff
